title: Don't Tell Kids "It Will Be Okay."
subtitle: Learn validation, not reassurance, to be a good parent or role model for kids...and adults.
body_html:
The world can be really scary. In case you haven't noticed, things might not be all right. For its worth, this includes up to “everything.” The problem with reassurance, especially when it comes to providing it to children, is that if “everything” does not end up all right, you are not only not the kind of help you were seeking to be, but you're a liar.

Newsflash: children hate liars. Let’s spend a moment on reassurance. Reassurance is the gummy peaches of human interaction. What I mean by that, of course, is that gummy peaches are delicious. They are sugary, they are sweet, and you don't want to eat them all day. You don't want to eat them every day. You want to have gummy peaches only occasionally. No responsible parent would give children less gummy peaches instead of nutritious food, because it would give your children diabetes, obesity, and all manner of ills.

One gummy won't kill you. Infrequent gummy peaches are not the end of the world. But any dreadfully sweet candy is just not an every day treat. You should save them, make them infrequent, and you should do the same thing with reassurance.

Children are frequently anxious. Adults are also frequently anxious. One of the ways we deal with that anxiety is often by looking to others and trying to assess whether we should be scared. The sweet, sugary, addictive version of “addressing anxiety”—that is not particularly healthy—is reflexively telling a child that it's gonna be fine. In the moment, this feels good. The length of that moment, in which the good feelings last, can be highly variable. It would be delightful if reassurance just lasted forever. Feel anxious, you ask them if it'll be OK, they tell you it it'll be OK, and then you're done. You're not anxious anymore!

If ONLY.

This is not how anxiety works. That feeling of anxiety, nervousness, it's really potent, it exists to keep us alive, to keep us on edge, so that we can mobilize our biological systems to fight or fight and get the hell out of there before we die. That system, mediated by our sympathetic nervous system, needs to work on a hair trigger all the time. Evolutionarily, the one time that system failed in any of our ancestors, that person was weeded out of the gene pool. Anxiety gets a little dose of reassurance, feels good, thanks to the trusted relationship. We have with the reassuring individual, but all of us who survived this day have had our fear system appropriately tuned to be worried again soon, if the threatening conditions persist. Which, in this day and age, they can be guaranteed to do. Most of the things were worried about, aren't gonna actually eat as alive like tigers, and yet we feel worried, like they might.

Reassurance— “You're fine!” It doesn't last—it’s the sugar high of addressing anxiety. Just like a sugar high, when it crashes, you couldn't find yourself wanting more. Reassurance feels good. Ask again.

Now you're on the loop. Another really common and terrible strategy is to help your child avoid what's making them anxious. Maybe they're worried about going to school? Maybe their stomach hurts because they're so worried about going to school. Maybe you should just let them stay home from school. Perhaps there's an adult, and they're worried about work, and now they're taking a day off because of their anxiety. Didn't you know they have chronic anxiety? Have you considered that what you said might be triggering? They're gonna need to avoid going to work or school because of their anxiety.

The strategy is also deeply problematic. When anxious people avoid something, they learn a valuable lesson: avoiding feels really good. If you avoid what they're afraid of, they don’t have to feel anxious at all. Anxious about dating? Don't go on a date. Test anxiety? Never take a test. Many of us as adults don't wanna push children who are anxious because it feels cruel to do so. Oftentimes, anxious children can throw really remarkable fits or scenes, so as to induce anxiety in adults, and the adults do what they want them to do. This is often a very successful strategy. Anxious children are the masters of manipulating anxious adults. We want to avoid their anxiety, and so we learned to help them avoid the things they're anxious about. It's an unspoken agreement, and a collaborative effort that is never said out loud, but definitely works reliably together. Children are awesome at manipulating adults. Adults, sadly, lag behind children in their ability to get their kids to do what they hope will be the best outcome.

What, then, good Doctor Muir, do you suggest any of us with anxious children should do not to be terrible parents or caregivers? Do you propose we just let our children suffer?

That would be intolerable!

The first thing I'd want to do is remind you that your children are smart, and they're getting what they need out of the world. Their anxiety makes perfect sense to them. They're afraid, and if they act afraid enough in front of an adult, they're not gonna have to to do the scary thing, which is a completely adaptive response if you're a scared child. The downside of avoidance is that you spend all day locked in a box, going nowhere, and doing nothing, at its extreme. You're too anxious to go to work, you never have a job. If you're too anxious to go to school, you can never learn that school can actually be fun and engaging. If you're too anxious to go on a date, you'll never meet that person who is quirky and cute, and kind of into you, and then you get married, and you have your own anxious kids to manage.

We need to be strategic to help our children facing anxieties.

Here is what I would recommend: instead of being reassuring, start by being validating. I'll give you an example.

“Dad, I don’t want to go into the store.”

Bad Dad version: “There is nothing to be afraid of, just get in there.”

Worse Dad version: “You know what, let's just go home, don't worry about it!”

Or, welcome our hero, Validating Dad!

Validating Dad: “Wait, what are you afraid of?”

Kid: “I’m afraid they will think I look bad.”

Validating Dad: “I’m confused—who? And what are they going to think looks bad?”

Kid: “My shorts! Ryan goes to this same Wegmans, he told me so. I spilled chocolate on them! It looks like poop.”

Validating Dad: “Oh my! It appears you did…”

And now here is the crucial moment, it can be really tempting to provide reassurance. Even, and especially if, it's factual. Now, normally, this will go fine. Reassurance is like gummy, peaches, as long as you don't use it too often, your kid will believe you, and it'll be fine. But for anxious children, who are constantly seeking reassurance, it stops serving its intended purpose and gets in the way of development.

The key here is leaning into, not knowing. Because kids can't learn to face their fears if they worry that they have to to be certain. Reassurance lies in certainty, and great parenting leans into uncertainty and “not knowing.” Just follow along:

Not-Knowing Super Dad (NKSD): “I'm not sure if Ryan will be there. Also, it's hard to know if anybody else will notice the chocolate on your shorts.”

Kid: “This is what I’m saying! Can you just go in instead?”

NKSD: “what do you imagine Ryan's gonna say if he sees the chocolate on your shorts?”

Kid: “I pooped my pants.”

NKSD: “imagine that would be an embarrassing thing for someone to say!”

Kid: “YES! IT would.”

NKSD: “but what if Ryan isn't in there?”

Kid: “any other kid is nicer than Ryan.”

NKSD: “Is there any way you could deal with it if Ryan saw you, even if he said that thing?”

Kid: “die of anxiety.”

NKSD: “how anxious are dead people?”

Kid: “I don’t know.”

NKSD: “Not so certain now?”

Kid: “I guess that people don't worry about much.”

NKSD: “I don't think they do either. So even in the worst case scenario, you would die of anxiety, but then you wouldn't care anymore?”

Kid: “I guess not.”

NKSD: “Let's go see what kind of chocolate they have. If we're lucky, I'll spill some on my shorts too, and we'll start a trend.”

Anxiety can ruin childhood. The parents can make it worse, or parents can make it better. Reassurance doesn't make anxiety better, it makes it worse. Avoidance doesn't make anxiety. Better, it makes it worse. Coping skills help children deal with anxiety better, and they basically learn those coping skills from watching their parents use them. One of the best things you can do is be as anxious as you actually are, say it out loud, and then use a coping skill, calm down, and do it all in front of your kids, when things are really stressful for you, personally, really. That's the best lesson you can teach. You can also avoid making it worse, but not helping them avoid things when they're anxious, and by not avoiding things, obviously, and out loud, in front of them when you're anxious.

Anxiety is a learned behavior. Anxious kids are good learners. Accidentally teaching in the wrong lessons, which are asked for reassurance, and avoiding things when you're anxious.

Being a great parent is about navigating your children's anxiety, and more importantly, navigating your own anxiety successfully by facing your fears head-on, avoiding reassurance, and being validating and curious when anxiety rears its head.
